#philosophy #epistemics

Edmund Gettier, "Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?", *Analysis* 23(6), 1963, pp. 121 to 123. Three pages, written, the story goes, because Wayne State wanted him to publish something. Case I: Smith has strong evidence that Jones will get the job and that Jones has ten coins in his pocket, so he believes "the man who gets the job has ten coins in his pocket". Smith gets the job, and unknown to him he also has ten coins. Justified, true, believed, and plainly not knowledge. Case II: Ford owns a car, or Brown is in Barcelona. Older cousins: Russell's stopped clock (1948), Chisholm's sheep in the field. My own, 21 Feb 2025: I told Aoife "the 46A is due in three minutes" from the app, the app had frozen, and a 46A turned up three minutes later anyway. It was luck, not knowledge. Responses worth a lesson: the no-false-lemmas fix, Goldman's causal theory (1967), and Zagzebski's 1994 paper arguing such cases are inescapable for any theory that lets justification fall short of truth. See also [[Plato's cave]] and [[Ship of Theseus]].
